title: Geometric Characterization of Maximal Cuts in Three-Loop Graviton-Scalar Worldline Integrals: Elliptic, K3, and Calabi-Yau Threefold Sector
content: We analyze the Baikov representations and maximal cuts of three-loop (4PM) graviton-scalar conservative and radiative master integrals in Worldline Quantum Field Theory (WQFT) extended to massive scalar-tensor and dilaton-gravity models. Employing a sequential loop-by-loop (LBL) Baikov parametrization that preserves eikonal momentum conservation on both heavy worldlines, we derive the cut Gram-determinant polynomials for representative nine-propagator master topologies with n ∈ {1, 2, 3} remaining Irreducible Scalar Products (ISPs). We show how dimensionless internal mass ratios χi = \( {m_i}^2 \) /t control the algebraic geometry, singular thresholds, and monodromy groups of the maximal cuts. For n = 1, massive triangle-box worldline ladders define χ-deformed elliptic curves (CY1) with mass-deformed modular cross-ratios λ(γ, χ) = 4χ/[γ2(4χ + 1) − 1] that remain smooth throughout the physical scattering region. For n = 2, graviton-scalar ladders define (P1)2 bidegree-(4, 4) K3 surfaces (CY2) whose Picard rank jumps from ρ = 18 (governed by a fourth-order SO(2, 2) Picard-Fuchs system) for unequal effective mass parameters to ρ = 19 (governed by a closed-form χ-dependent third-order Sym2SL(2) operator) in the symmetric limit. For n = 3, nine-propagator non-planar graviton-scalar topologies with (E1, E2, E3) = (3, 3, 3) define (P1)3 multi-degree-(4, 4, 4) double-cover threefolds (CY3). We demonstrate that while equal-rung topologies reduce birationally to conic bundles, unequal scalar rung masses obstruct this trivialization and generate a compact S3 vanishing cycle. We validate the period expansions of the unequal-mass K3 ladder, the unequal-rung CY3 topology, and its symmetric (4, 4, 4) Sp(4, Z) benchmark against numerical quadrature to 12 digits, analyze conservative versus Schwinger-Keldysh radiative homology projections, and construct ϵ-factorized canonical differential equations.
